Understanding Tenant Rights and Responsibilities

As a tenant, you have certain rights and responsibilities when it comes to electricity and other utilities in your rental unit. Understanding these rights and responsibilities can help you avoid disputes with your landlord and ensure that you are not taken advantage of.
Lease Agreement and Utility Clauses

Your lease agreement should outline the terms of your tenancy, including who is responsible for paying for utilities such as electricity. In most cases, the landlord is responsible for paying for the electricity used in common areas, while tenants are responsible for paying for the electricity they use in their individual units.

It is important to carefully review your lease agreement to understand your responsibilities for utility payments. If you have any questions or concerns, you should discuss them with your landlord before signing the lease.
Legal Protections for Tenants

Tenants have legal protections when it comes to utility services. In Missouri, the Utility Services Tenants Right Act requires that tenants be notified by the utility company at least 30 days in advance if the landlord fails to pay the utility bill or instructs the utility company to shut off service. Once the utilities have been shut off, the situation must be remedied within 72 hours.

Additionally, landlords must perform necessary repairs in a timely manner. If repairs aren't made in a reasonable time after getting notice from tenants, Missouri tenants can sue for costs or a court order to force the landlord to make repairs.
Responsibilities for Utility Payments
As a tenant, you are responsible for paying for the electricity you use in your individual unit. It is important to pay your utility bills on time to avoid late fees or service interruptions.

Electricity and Utility Services in Rental Units

As a tenant, it's important to understand your rights regarding electricity and other utility services in your rental unit. This section will cover the types of utilities you may encounter, how to deal with utility interruptions, and utility allowances and submetering.
Types of Utilities

Electricity is one of the most important utility services in a rental unit. Other common utilities include gas, water, and internet/cable services. It's important to know which utilities are included in your rent and which ones you are responsible for paying separately.
Dealing with Utility Interruptions

If your utility services are interrupted, it's important to know your rights. In most cases, the utility company is required to give you notice before shutting off your service. If your service is shut off without notice, you may be able to take legal action against the utility company.
Utility Allowances and Submetering

Some landlords may offer utility allowances as part of your rent. This means that a portion of your rent is allocated to cover your utility costs. However, if you exceed the allowance, you may be responsible for paying the additional costs.

Submetering is another option for utility management. This involves installing individual meters in each rental unit to measure usage. This can be beneficial for both landlords and tenants, as it allows for more accurate billing and can encourage tenants to be more conscious of their energy usage.

Rights Related to Utility Bills and Payments
As a tenant, it is important to understand your rights related to utility bills and payments. This section will cover some of the most important aspects of this topic.
Understanding Your Utility Bill

Your utility bill will typically include charges for electricity, gas, water, and possibly other services such as heat, sewer, telephone, or internet. It is important to understand how these charges are calculated and what fees may be added to your bill. In some cases, you may be eligible for a utility allowance to help cover these costs.
Addressing Overcharges and Disputes

If you believe that you have been overcharged on your utility bill or have a dispute with your utility company, there are steps you can take to address the issue. You may be able to file a complaint with your state's Public Service Commission or other regulatory agency. In addition, you may be able to negotiate a payment plan or seek assistance from a utility assistance program.
Payment Plans and Assistance Programs

If you are having difficulty paying your utility bills, you may be eligible for a payment plan or assistance program. Many utility companies offer payment plans that allow you to spread out your payments over a longer period of time. In addition, there are a variety of assistance programs available that can help lower your bills or provide financial assistance.

As specialists in sub-metering for a diverse range of real estate investments, we can help you save money and increase the value of your property. With an average property value increase of 32% and lower operating costs of 18%, we are the best option for Utility Management. Plus, we are 100% regulatory compliant, so you can be confident that you are in good hands.
Maintenance and Repairs of Electrical Systems

As a tenant, it's essential to understand your rights when it comes to electrical systems in your rental property. Electrical problems can be dangerous and require prompt attention. In this section, we'll cover the landlord's responsibility for repairs, your role in maintenance, and when to report electrical problems.
Landlord's Responsibility for Repairs

Landlords are responsible for ensuring that the electrical system in your rental unit is safe and functional. This includes repairing any electrical problems that arise during your tenancy. If you experience any issues with your electrical system, you should report them to your landlord immediately.
According to
FindLaw

, landlords are required to maintain habitable rental properties. This means that they must ensure that the electrical system is safe and functional. If your landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may have legal options available to you.
Tenant's Role in Maintenance

As a tenant, you have a role to play in maintaining the electrical system in your rental unit. You should ensure that you're not overloading circuits and that you're using appliances correctly. If you notice any issues with your electrical system, you should report them to your landlord immediately.
According to
RentPrep

, tenants are responsible for repairing any damage they cause to the electrical system. However, it's essential to note that tenants should not attempt to make electrical repairs themselves. Electrical repairs should only be performed by a licensed electrician.
When to Report Electrical Problems

If you experience any electrical problems in your rental unit, you should report them to your landlord immediately. Electrical problems can be dangerous and require prompt attention. Examples of electrical problems that should be reported include:
Flickering lights
Outlets that don't work
Circuit breakers that trip frequently
Burning smells or sparks coming from outlets or switches
Reporting electrical problems promptly can help prevent more significant issues from arising and keep you safe.

Legal Recourse and Protection Against Retaliation

As a tenant, you have legal rights that protect you from retaliation by your landlord. If you believe that your landlord has acted in retaliation against you, you have the right to take legal action. In this section, we will discuss the legal recourse available to you and the protections provided by the law.
Eviction and Utility Shut-off Laws

Your landlord cannot evict you or shut off your utilities in retaliation for asserting your legal rights as a tenant. If your landlord attempts to do so, you may have legal recourse. The laws governing eviction and utility shut-offs vary by state, so it is important to consult with a legal professional or your local Department of Public Utilities (DPU) for guidance on your specific situation.
Protection for Vulnerable Tenants

Disabled, elderly, and families with children are considered vulnerable tenants and are afforded additional protections under the law. Landlords must make reasonable accommodations for tenants with disabilities, such as installing wheelchair ramps or allowing service animals. Additionally, landlords cannot discriminate against families with children by refusing to rent to them or evicting them because of their children.
Seeking Legal Assistance

If you believe that your landlord has retaliated against you, seeking legal assistance may be your best course of action. The National Consumer Law Center is a valuable resource for tenants seeking legal advice and representation. Additionally, many states have legal aid organizations that provide free or low-cost legal services to low-income tenants.
